Let N≥99 be the eligible negative pool, n=99, and K the negatives ranked ahead of the target under the evaluator’s tie rule. The sampled outranking count X is hypergeometric: P(X=x)=C(K,x)C(N−K,n−x)/C(N,n). Thus exact expected HR@10 is P(X≤9), and expected negative-win fraction is E[X/n]=K/N. Its variance is (K/N)(1−K/N)(N−n)/[n(N−1)]. These are direct applications of [sampling without replacement](https://www.mathworks.com/help/stats/hypergeometric-distribution.html); score ties must match the evaluator’s ranking policy.

Sort all negative scores s₍₁₎≤…≤s₍N₎. The sampled maximum M satisfies P(M≤t)=C(A(t),n)/C(N,n), where A(t) counts pool scores ≤t. Consequently E[M]=Σⱼ₌ₙᴺ s₍ⱼ₎C(j−1,n−1)/C(N,n); this remains valid with tied scores. These combinatorial formulas follow from [finite-population order statistics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.00270). Scoring the complete eligible pool therefore replaces five-draw estimates with exact sampling expectations; average per-user expectations within categories, then macro-average categories.

Exact expectations have no candidate-sampling Monte Carlo error, although user-sampling and model-training uncertainty remain separate. For Monte Carlo estimates, count independent candidate-set draws only: reusing an earlier frozen set supplies no additional replication, and repeating deterministic scoring cannot reduce its uncertainty. Report the realized frozen-set result separately from the sampling expectation. Fresh independent draws permit standard errors across draws; reused sets across models support paired comparisons, with covariance retained. If the model was selected using that frozen set, fresh draws or exact finite-pool calculations avoid interpreting selection-conditioned performance as an unbiased sampling estimate.
